title: Given the root of a binary tree, invert it so that the left and right children of every node are swapped, producing a mirror image of the original tree.
shortTitle: Invert/Mirror Binary Tree — swap left and right recursively

s1_definition.profdef: Inverting a binary tree produces its mirror image by swapping the left and right child of every node. The standard solution is a recursive traversal that, at each node, swaps its two children and then recursively inverts both subtrees, so the entire structure is flipped horizontally.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has an org chart drawn on glass, and he wants to see how it looks from the other side, as a mirror image. At every manager, the person who was on the left now appears on the right and vice versa. He does this swap at the top, then repeats it for each sub-team all the way down. The result is the same chart flipped left-to-right.
s1_definition.oneliner: At every node swap its two children, then recursively invert both subtrees.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Inverting a binary tree produces its mirror image by swapping the left and right child of every node. The standard solution is a recursive traversal that, at each node, swaps its two children and then recursively inverts both subtrees, so the entire structure is flipped horizontally.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has an org chart drawn on glass, and he wants to see how it looks from the other side, as a mirror image. At every manager, the person who was on the left now appears on the right and vice versa. He does this swap at the top, then repeats it for each sub-team all the way down. The result is the same chart flipped left-to-right.

**One line to remember:** At every node swap its two children, then recursively invert both subtrees.

sections.s2_technical:
Inverting a tree is a transformation rather than a query, so instead of returning a measurement you mutate the structure. The operation is recursive because inverting a tree means swapping the root's children and then inverting each child subtree.

The base case is a null node, which has nothing to invert, so you return it unchanged. For example: `if (node == null) return null;`.

The core step is swapping the two children at the current node. For example: `Node temp = node.left; node.left = node.right; node.right = temp;`. After the swap, you recursively invert both subtrees. For example: `invert(node.left); invert(node.right);`.

The order of swapping versus recursing does not change the final result, because the swap at a node is independent of the swaps deeper down. You can swap first then recurse, or recurse first then swap; both produce the same fully mirrored tree. What matters is that every node performs exactly one swap.

The time complexity is linear because every node is visited once and performs a constant-time swap. The space is proportional to the height from the recursion stack. A senior nuance is the iterative alternative using a queue or stack, which visits each node and swaps its children without recursion, avoiding stack-overflow risk on very deep trees. Another nuance is to decide whether the operation should mutate the input tree in place or build and return a new inverted tree, which depends on whether the caller still needs the original.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a reporting hierarchy is stored with primary approvers on the left and backup approvers on the right. For a disaster-recovery drill, the operations team needs the mirror version where backups become primary, which is exactly a left-right swap at every node. This is exactly how Invert Binary Tree works.

Problem 2 — The drill must flip the entire chain, not just the top, so every level must be swapped consistently. This is exactly why the inversion recurses into both subtrees after swapping at each node.

The mini-project builds an `ApproverNode` class, an `HierarchyInverterService` with a recursive `invert` method and logging, and a runnable demo that inverts a small hierarchy and prints a pre-order traversal before and after.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the hierarchy rooted at Manager, with PrimaryCredit on the left and BackupCredit on the right.

Step 1: The service calls invert on Manager. It swaps Manager's children, so BackupCredit moves to the left and PrimaryCredit moves to the right.

Step 2: It recursively inverts Manager's new left child, BackupCredit. BackupCredit had a right child BackupJr and no left child. After the swap, BackupJr moves to the left and the right becomes null.

Step 3: It recurses into BackupCredit's children. The new left child BackupJr has no children, so its swap does nothing. The new right child is null, so that call returns immediately.

Step 4: It recursively inverts Manager's new right child, PrimaryCredit. PrimaryCredit had a left child PrimaryJr and no right child. After the swap, PrimaryJr moves to the right and the left becomes null.

Step 5: It recurses into PrimaryCredit's children. PrimaryJr has no children, so nothing changes, and the null side returns immediately.

Step 6: Every node has been swapped. The pre-order traversal now shows BackupCredit on the left and PrimaryCredit on the right, with their own children mirrored too.

```text
2026-10-26T17:50:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — DR Drill Hierarchy Inversion

2026-10-26T17:50:00Z [INFO] Running DR drill: inverting approver hierarchy (primary <-> backup)
2026-10-26T17:50:00Z [INFO] Inversion complete: backups are now primary at every level
2026-10-26T17:50:00Z [INFO] After:  Manager(BackupCredit(BackupJr(_,_),_),PrimaryCredit(_,PrimaryJr(_,_)))
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Inverting a binary tree is a transformation rather than a query, so instead of returning a measurement I mutate the structure to produce its mirror image. The operation is naturally recursive: at each node I swap its left and right children, then recursively invert both subtrees. The base case is a null node, which has nothing to swap, so I simply return.

An important point I make in interviews is that the order of swapping versus recursing does not matter, because the swap at any given node is independent of the swaps happening deeper in the tree. Whether I swap first and then recurse, or recurse first and then swap, every node performs exactly one swap and the final mirrored tree is identical. What matters is that no node is missed and none is swapped twice.

The time complexity is linear because every node is visited once and does a constant-time swap, and the space is proportional to the tree height from the recursion stack. For very deep trees I would offer the iterative version using a queue or stack that swaps each node's children without recursion, which avoids any stack-overflow risk. I would also clarify with the interviewer whether to mutate in place or return a new tree, depending on whether the original is still needed.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this in a disaster-recovery drill service. The approval hierarchy stores primary approvers on the left and backups on the right, and the drill needs the mirror version where backups become primary at every level. The recursive swap flips the entire chain consistently, and we persist the mirrored tree as a drill snapshot so operations can validate that backup approvers are correctly wired before a real failover.
